summary: Cetus is an offline field tool for a Mars astronaut on a surface EVA, built in Qt 6 and C++17 around real NASA data from Gale Crater. It loads a HiRISE orthoimage and stereo terrain model, derives slope, and builds a hazard grid where steep or missing-data terrain is never treated as safe. From that it ranks science targets, plans a hazard-avoiding traverse, and enforces a walkback rule: the crew must always be able to return to the start within the EVA time limit, with a slower-return factor and a reserve. A scripted scenario replans live, and crew can add their own points. The plan includes an estimated radiation dose from Curiosity’s MSL RAD measurements, and one click logs a geotagged field note with terrain orientation. The hard part of EVA planning is knowing when to turn back, so Cetus makes that limit visible. It is also upfront about gaps: oxygen, power and water are not modeled, and every tuning value is labeled a design choice, not a NASA value.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?
Cetus is an offline field tool for a Mars astronaut on a surface EVA (extravehicular activity), built around real NASA data from Gale Crater. It loads a HiRISE orthoimage and stereo terrain model, derives slope, and builds a 10 m hazard grid where slopes above 20° or missing data count as no-go, never as safe. It ranks science targets by value per minute, plans a hazard-weighted A* traverse, and chains several targets into one plan. Its core is the walkback rule: elapsed time + leg + work + 1.2 × return + 15 min reserve must fit the EVA limit (6 h by default, editable). The map draws the full plan and the way home. A scripted scenario (dust rising, storm cuts the budget to 90 min, comms offline, power low) replans live. The crew can add their own points, switch to a one-way trip, see an estimated radiation dose for the planned EVA, and log a geotagged field note with terrain orientation.

2. What benefits does it have?
It shows when to turn back, the decision a crew cannot afford to get wrong. It works with no network at run time, flags every limit it cannot verify, and gives one clear next target with the reason.

3. What is the intended impact?
A decision-support prototype for EVA traverse planning, training and analog studies. It is not a certified navigation system.

4. Tools, languages, hardware, software

  • C++17 and Qt 6 (Widgets), CMake, GDAL and PROJ, Qt Test with ctest; developed on a Linux desktop, no special hardware.
  • NASA data: MRO HiRISE orthoimage and stereo DTM, NASA Mars Trek waypoints, MSL RAD surface dose rate (Hassler et al., Science, 2014).
  • Git/GitHub; AI coding assistants were used during development.

5. How is it creative?
It puts the return trip first: the way home is planned and drawn as a best path, not a retrace. It is honest by design, with every tuning value marked as a design choice, unknown terrain treated as no-go, and a sample record described as a field note, not a measured sample.

6. What factors did the team consider?
Data honesty: we found and fixed a slope-unit error (percent instead of degrees) that would have triggered the 20° rule at about 11°. We used a Mars coordinate system, not WGS84. Missing data stays unknown. Limits are stated openly: oxygen, power and water are not modeled, crew movement is not simulated, and the 4 m slope smooths boulders. NASA’s 6±2 h EVA range comes from lunar (Artemis) documents; no Mars suit spec exists yet.
